Let's Examine the Extraordinary Cancer Recoveries of Ruth Ginsberg

The 86-year-old Ruth Bader Ginsburg had already had two bouts of cancer: colon cancer in 1999; pancreatic cancer in 2009; lung cancer in 2018.

Let’s examine the colon cancer survival rate to a then 66 year old Ginsburg.

The SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results) database is used by the American Cancer Society to provide statistical information on survival rates for pancreatic cancer. It is categorized into 4 groupings – Localized, Regional, Distant, and Combined.

The SEER database, however, does not group cancers by AJCC TNM stages (stage 1, stage 2, stage 3, etc.). Instead, it groups cancers into localized, regional, and distant stages:

For Colon Cancer the SEER Database has the following data:

Localized – 5-yr Relative Survival Rate is 90%

Regional – 5-yr Relative Survival Rate is 71%

Distant – 5-yr Relative Survival Rate is 14%

All SEER stages combined – 5-yr Relative Survival Rate is 64%

Again, age affects the recovery of cancer patients.

Ginburg’s survival of colon cancer for a 66 year old female is somewhat plausible, especially if the patient is physically fit. However, age affects the recovery of cancer patients. The older a cancer patient the less likely their survival.

Ginsburg was 76 years old when she was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. It should be noted that more than half of all cases of pancreatic cancer are first diagnosed at stage 4.

For Pancreatic Cancer the SEER Database has the following data:

Localized – 5-yr Relative Survival Rate is 34%

Regional – 5-yr Relative Survival Rate is 12%

Distant – 5-yr Relative Survival Rate is 3%

All SEER stages combined – 5-yr Relative Survival Rate is 9%

Age affects the recovery of cancer patients. The older a cancer patient the less likely their survival. Even if the 5-yr. Survival Rate is 34% elderly age will affect this.

Ginburg’s survival of pancreatic cancer for a 76 year old female is was somewhat miraculous. It is in all probability the spread of the malignancy of the first cancer she had 10 years before.

Broken Ribs and Lung Cancer

In 2018, the 85 year old Ginsburg was diagnosed with lung cancer discovered after she broke her ribs in an apparent fall. The extent of Ginsburg’s injury was not clear at press time. Rib fractures are common among older adults, particularly after falls. The severity depends in part on whether the ribs are cracked or broken all the way through, and how many are broken.

It is reported that surgery was performed to remove the lower portion of her cancerous left lung. It was not reported however, what type of lung cancer was found.

It is most likely that the cancer found in the left lung was a lung metastases. Lung metastasis is cancer that started from another area (i.e. colon, pancreas) and has spread to the lung. It is not the same as cancer that starts in the lung (called primary lung cancer).

Not everyone with lung metastases can have surgery. It depends on the size, number and location of tumours, how well the primary cancer is controlled, your overall health and other factors (like age). Ginsberg is reported to having surgery though.

Indeed, it was most likely not a primary lung cancer, but rather a lung metastases. For an 85 year old woman, her survival from surgery has to be remarkable. I am not factoring in her broken ribs, which would also be a concern to perform surgery.

Her survival of 3 cancers, one being considered a very aggressive and deadly form -- pancreatic cancer, is nothing less than incredible.
